stubs.angle: Asks which aspect of a pull request Google's code review guide calls the most important thing to check.
stubs.answerHinge: The guide names the overall design of the change as the most important thing to cover, ahead of style, naming or comments.

stubs.angle: Asks which statements about the Daily Scrum are true according to the 2020 Scrum Guide.
stubs.answerHinge: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog, and the 2020 guide does not prescribe the three questions or make it a status report to a manager.

stubs.angle: Asks why planning poker has everyone reveal their estimate at the same time and what the team should do when estimates differ widely.
stubs.answerHinge: A simultaneous reveal prevents anchoring on the first voice, and a wide spread signals different assumptions that the high and low estimators should explain before the team estimates again.

stubs.subtopic: Code review from the author's side
stubs.angle: The author of a pull request gets a reviewer comment they believe is wrong and feels irritated; what do they do?
stubs.answerHinge: The author first considers whether the reviewer is right, replies without anger, and when the reviewer misread the code clarifies the code itself instead of only explaining in the review thread.

stubs.angle: A middle developer on their first on-call shift is paged at night for an alert in a service they do not know; what do they do?
stubs.answerHinge: Acknowledge the page, follow the runbook and escalate early along the agreed path instead of trying to solve an unfamiliar incident alone.

stubs.angle: A teammate repeatedly rewrites code you merged without telling you; how do you handle it?
stubs.answerHinge: Under collective code ownership changing others' code is legitimate, so the problem is the missing communication: raise it privately with concrete examples and agree on a team norm instead of reverting or escalating first.

stubs.angle: During a major outage five engineers debug in one chat channel, nobody updates stakeholders and two people roll back conflicting changes; what do you do?
stubs.answerHinge: Declare an incident with explicit roles - an incident commander who coordinates and decides, an operations lead who changes the system and a communications lead who updates stakeholders - so coordination is separated from fixing and only agreed changes are made.

stubs.angle: Retrospectives keep producing the same complaints and long action lists that nobody completes; what do you do?
stubs.answerHinge: Pick the one or two most impactful improvements, give each an owner and put it into the next sprint's work, then check the result at the next retrospective.

stubs.angle: Asks how to improve forecasts when the team's estimates are consistently about half the actual time.
stubs.answerHinge: Calibrate forecasts on measured historical throughput or velocity instead of padding each new guess, and treat velocity as a planning tool, not a productivity target.

stubs.angle: Asks how a senior developer should structure the first weeks of a new team member so they become productive.
stubs.answerHinge: Have the newcomer ship a small real change early by pairing on actual tasks with a named buddy, instead of weeks of reading documentation alone.

stubs.angle: After an integration outage two teams blame each other in chat and each says the other broke the contract; how do you mediate?
stubs.answerHinge: Replace the question of whose fault it is with a shared factual timeline in one joint, blameless session that ends with a jointly owned fix for the interface between the teams.

stubs.angle: Asks how a lead reduces long cycle times when every developer has three or four tasks in progress at once.
stubs.answerHinge: Limiting work in progress shortens cycle time, so the team agrees explicit WIP limits and finishes started work before pulling new work, even though utilisation looks lower.
